title: Acquisition, durability and transfer are separate claims
statement: Treat acquisition, durable mastery and transfer as three claims, each needing its own evidence, and never let a check built for one stand in for another.
example: One course set acquisition at 90% on 15 distinct new feedback-free items, and durable mastery at 80% or more on a different day.
detail: A Grade 5 reading course's BrainLift states that acquisition, durable mastery and transfer are different claims, and that a same-session checkpoint cannot establish durability (`incept-package-hub/course-packages/courses/g5-reading/review/brainlift.html`). Its policy builds each theme checkpoint from fifteen distinct new certified items, at least three of them integrative, with no feedback and a ninety-percent acquisition threshold, and reserves durable-mastery claims for a different-day, feedback-free assessment on novel items at or above eighty percent (`incept-package-hub/course-packages/courses/g5-reading/source/canonical/pedagogy-policy.json`, lines 1719 and 1754). Transfer requires cold passages on never-taught topics and stays separate from course mastery or an impact claim. The scheme ties together three narrower rules: a later test on new items, a delay that is proven, and cold texts kept for testing.
against: A Grade 3 course's archived prompts made its cold-transfer lessons, on unseen texts within the unit's own topic, the unit exit gates: 'This is the unit exit gate (≥90%): passing means the child owns the tool,' (`incept-package-hub/course-packages/archive/g3-reading-v2/authoring/prompts/u01.md`, line 193), and the same course's assessment memo named those cold-transfer exit lessons as its real high-dependency gates. The Grade 5 scheme is a design: at its red-team review, all 550 of its items were still not certified.
